segments.text: Guanaco 3.8 is a new open model with 27
billion parameters and today I'm not
going to try to find out whether it can
replace Opus or Gemini. In my opinion,
comparing them directly isn't really the
right approach. I'm much more interested
in something else. How complex the real
world task be that you can give to a
local model of this size while still
being confident that it can handle them.
So I prepared several tests from a very
simple project to a complex application
with a front end, back end and database.
And as you will see later, at some point
the model really did hit its limit, but
I want to remind you that I don't see
local models as a complete replacement
for paid ones. For me, they are an
additional tools for relatively simple
and routine tasks as well as for cases
where I don't want my data to leave my
computer. So today I want to determine
what tasks I can already safely trust
Guanaco 3.8 with and what it's still
better to left to larger models.
By the way, the main computer I'm
currently working on is a MacBook, but
it has only 24 GB of unified memory and
unfortunately that's not enough to
comfortably run today's model. The model
does run on it, but it works very
slowly, which is clearly not enough for
normal use. So I'll be using Guanaco 3.8
on my desktop and using it from my
MacBook over the local network. On the
screen you can see the specs of this
desktop. If you also decide to run
Guanaco 3.8, the main thing to pay
attention to is having a GPU with as
much memory as possible. This is the
most important parameter for running LLM
models. So first I download this model
to my desktop. To run the model, I'll be
using Ollama, but you can use any other
inference tool. For example, LM Studio
or Ollama CPP, which I also use quite
often. Now, just to make sure I check
whether it works. Yes, everything is
fine. The model has been downloaded,
launched it and is working. Now I'll
create a separate folder where I run the
tests with this model. For the tests,
I'll use my repository with a collection
of prompts. They are grouped from simple
to complex and I run them in that order.
By the way, this repository is available
on GitHub. So you can download it and
experiment with it. As the agent, I'll
be using pie. I really like it because
of how minimalistic and extensible it
is. And in my opinion, it gives you the
most direct access to the model, if I
can put it that way.
So for the first test, I'll use a task
to create an HTML page with a clock,
stopwatch and timer. And [clears throat]
I simply ask the model to implement this
project. Since this is the easiest task,
I won't create any plan and will just
ask it to build the project based on the
description. Okay, the model has started
thinking and while we're waiting for the
result, I'll open a new tab and check
how much load actively using this model
put on my desktop. So ignore the graph
on the left. It belongs to the
integrated GPU, which is not being used

the one running the quant model. As you
can see, the entire model fits into the
GPU memory and there is still plenty of
room left for a large context window.
The GPU is fully loaded. Great.
Okay, I won't show the entire response
generation process because it may take a
while. I'll just tell you at the end how
long it took. So quant says that it has
finished working on this project.
Generating the response and creating the
file took in just over 3 minutes. Pretty

Well, it looks pretty good. There is
clock, a stopwatch and a timer. The
buttons work and everything behaves
exactly as I expected. It looks like all
the functionality works correctly. We
can confidently say that Gwen completed
this project successfully. So, it's time
to move on to a more difficult task. And
for a more difficult task, I'll use a
Pomodoro timer project. There is a
reason why this project is one level
more complex. It has a hidden
difficulty. The timer has several
different states and the app needs to
detect them correctly and transition
between them properly. Browser
notifications also need to work.
Analytics and settings need to be saved.
And of course, nice animations are also
one of the requirements. Usually, for
medium complexity task that I give to
local models, I first create an
implementation plan. Then, the model
follows that plan step by step and
implement the project. However, for
today's model, I want to make it a bit
more challenging and try to implement
this task without a plan as well, just
based on the description. Let's see if
it can handle it. Again, let's quickly
check the system load while it is
generating the response. Yes, everything
looks the same as the first time. The
GPU is handling all the load. Excellent.
Now, we just need to wait for the
result. Okay, so Gwen 3.8 says that it

response took twice as long as with the
simple task, around 6 minutes. I think
it's a good result. Now, I open it in
the browser. Wow, it looks great. I
didn't expect the design to look this
good and apparently, everything works.
There are no errors. I'm very happy that
the model managed to do this literally
from the first prompt. To be honest, I
didn't expect such a good result. I am
impressed. So, I think now it's time to
move on to an even more difficult task.
After today's model handled the first
tasks without any problems. I decided to
give it a much more difficult
assignment. This time, I need to create
not only the front end, but also the
back end. It will also require active
work with a database. So, the project
will be a news feed aggregator. But to
make the task even more difficult, I
decided that the entry project should be
written in the Nim programming language.
If you have never heard of this
language, that's perfectly fine.
Unfortunately, it is still not very
popular. However, I really like it, so I
experiment with it from time to time.
Okay, since trying to implement a
project like this with a single prompt
would be pointless, I'll organize the
work in the following way. I have a
project description. First, I'll use the

following this approach, I'll ask the

So, after a few minutes, the plan is

give the project description and the

GPT 5.6. So, let's see if there are any

Yeah, unfortunately, the larger model
found six critical issues in the

plan as conceptually good, which is
already not bad, but not ready for
implementation.
Well, it looks like I have found the
first limitation of today's model. It is
not suitable for complex architecture
and project planning tasks, which is
basically what I expected considering
its size, but it was still interesting
to test. Now, I want to test it on the
kind of task I usually give to models
like this, namely the sequential
implementation of many clearly defined
programming tasks as part of building a
project. For this, I refined the
implementation plan together with
ChatGPT, and I split it into small
tasks.
Now, I simply go through the list of
task with the model and give them to it
one by one. Let's see how well Gwen
handled this. So, the whole process is
finally complete. Overall, it took me
around 2 hours. Sometimes I had to
correct the model and help it with
certain things, but overall, it
performed very well. Now, let's run the
application, and I'll show you what we
ended up with. But, I want to point out
that this is more of prototype than a
finished application. So, after
launching it, the front end opened
successfully. But, since I haven't added

according to the task, the service
should support fetching and saving
articles from RSS feeds. So, let's go
back to the main page. Oh, the articles

loaded. That means the back end worked
as expected, too. Great. I won't go into
the project source code in the detail.
I'll just upload it to GitHub, and if
you are interested, you'll be able to
explore it there. But, what about the
third task? Did the model handle it? In
my opinion, yes. Despite the unusual
programming language, it successfully
completed all the tasks, and in the end,
we got a fully working prototype of the
service. It includes asynchronous
network operations, as well as database
work. I think that is excellent result.
The fact that it couldn't design the
entire service on its own is completely
fine. After all, this is a relatively
small model that runs locally. It would
be strange to expect the same
capabilities from it as from large cloud
models. I also want to compare it
separately with its predecessor. In my
experience, this model is much more
capable. In my previous tests, Guanaco
3.6 struggled with my medium complexity
tasks. And even there, I already had to
split the work into smaller tasks. The
new Guanaco 3.8 handled them without any
problems, even from a single prompt. So,
the progress is obvious. And as a result
of today's tests, I can say that I
really like the model, and I'll
definitely upgrade to it from the
previous version. Let me know if you
have any comments if you already tried
